claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution.
Components inside a Pulumi package inherit the package's version.
Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), each versioned and released differently.
A source-based plugin package is distributed as source code in a Git repository.
A source-based Pulumi package's version is the Git tag on its repository.
Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow, typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
Publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry involves applying a semver Git tag (e.g., `v1.2.3`) to the repository.
Running `pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
The `pulumi package publish` step often runs automated tests before publishing.
Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds such as npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents.
An executable-based Pulumi package's version is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Releases of executable-based packages are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
In both the source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
Pulumi recommends that a repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type.
A repository containing multiple Pulumi packages must either release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that fights how Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are supported and expected, shipping together at the package's version.

Pulumi's recommended approach is to define exactly one package per repository, group a cohesive set of components inside that package, and use multiple repositories (one per package) to manage distinct packages.
The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with the supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
The Amazon EKS package is a good reference point for cohesive component grouping because its components are almost always used together and tend to evolve together.
It is technically possible to use a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components, but Pulumi does not recommend this approach.
Bundling unrelated components into a single package forfeits meaningful semantic versioning, which is how consumers know whether a given change is a bug fix, a new feature, or a breaking change.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way regardless of whether each component changed, violating semver.

In the illustrative example, a package containing ComponentA and ComponentB starts at v1.0.0 with both components at v1.0.0, then an enhancement to ComponentA alone bumps the package to v1.1.0, then a breaking change to ComponentB alone bumps the package to v2.0.0.
